title: Judaism: hear
hook: the central declaration: hear, O Israel, the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vesak, lanterns and a full moon to close our Buddhist visit. Your line was the full moon. Did you find the moon, and give something away? Day two hundred forty-six, and a new visit: Judaism.

Six Hebrew words. Observant Jews say them twice a day, morning and night, often with a hand over the eyes. They're whispered to children at bedtime. They're written on a tiny scroll inside a case on the doorframe of Jewish homes. And Jewish tradition hopes they will be among a person's last words. What's striking is the very first word. It isn't believe, or pray, or obey. It's listen. Today's word: Shema.
screen: `SIX HEBREW WORDS, TWICE A DAY.` → `ON THE DOORFRAME, AT BEDTIME.` → `SHEMA.`

segments.voice: The words come from the book of Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse four, where Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, it begins Shema Yisrael. Shema means hear, but it's a rich word: listen, pay attention, understand, take it to heart, even obey. It's hearing that changes what you do. And notice who's addressed. Not one person alone. Israel, the whole people. Then the verse that follows: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The passage goes on to say these words should be on your heart, taught to your children, spoken when you sit at home and walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up, bound on your hand and written on your doorposts. Observant Jews do exactly that. The Shema is said in the morning and evening prayers. It's written inside the mezuzah on the doorpost and inside tefillin, the small leather boxes some Jews bind on the arm and head for weekday morning prayer. The custom when saying it is to cover the eyes, shutting out everything else to listen. A guest's note: when Jews read the divine name, written in English as LORD, they don't pronounce it, but say Adonai, my Lord, instead. The Talmud tells of Rabbi Akiva, put to death by the Romans, dying with the Shema's last word, one, on his lips. The center of Jewish faith begins with an open ear.
screen: `DEUTERONOMY 6:4.` · `SHEMA: HEAR, HEED, TAKE TO HEART.` · `LIE DOWN, RISE UP, DOORPOSTS.` · `EYES COVERED, TO LISTEN.` · then, large: `HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen, for the length of the bell. Settle and breathe. If you like, cover your eyes with your hand, as is the custom for the Shema. Now just hear. The nearest sound. Then something farther away. The hum of the room. Your own breath. Don't name them or judge them. Just let hearing be the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Shema. Hebrew for hear, listen, take to heart: the first word of Judaism's central declaration, said morning and night. Today's word.
Your line: hear. Today, in one conversation, listen the way the Shema asks: fully, to take it to heart, not just to wait for your turn. Day two hundred forty-six.

fork.setup: you're a guest at a Jewish prayer service. everyone covers their eyes and says six words together. what do you do?
options: sit quietly and listen with them.
fork.reveal: the Shema is a moment of listening. a guest can simply be still and hear it; questions can wait until afterward.

what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 6:4–9 with 11:13–21 and Numbers 15:37–41 form the full Shema; the story of Rabbi Akiva is in Berakhot 61b.
